ideas.name: Light frees electrons
ideas.question: How does sunlight create moving electric charges in a solar cell?
ideas.modelAnswer: A photon with enough energy hits a bond in silicon and knocks an electron free, leaving a hole. The freed electron can then wander through the crystal.

ideas.name: The built-in slope
ideas.question: Why does the p–n junction make electrons flow in one direction?
ideas.modelAnswer: Where n-type and p-type silicon meet, a permanent electric field forms. It sweeps freed electrons to the n side and holes the other way, so a wire lets them flow round.

ideas.name: Inverter changes current
ideas.question: Why does a home solar system need an inverter?
ideas.modelAnswer: Panels make direct current that flows one way, but household sockets use alternating current that reverses many times a second. The inverter converts one into the other.

ideas.name: Why light is wasted
ideas.question: Why can a silicon panel never use all the sunlight?
ideas.modelAnswer: Photons with too little energy do nothing useful, and photons with extra energy shed the excess as heat. So one silicon layer can convert at most about a third of sunlight.

ideas.name: Cool and well aimed
ideas.question: Why do cool temperature and facing the Sun improve panel output?
ideas.modelAnswer: Heat makes atoms jiggle, which lowers each cell's voltage, so cold panels do better. A panel facing the Sun squarely catches more photons because the beam is not spread over more glass.

i4.say: Oh! So light that is too weak just zips straight past the silicon like it forgot to stop, and light that is too strong gives its extra fizz away as warm little sparks. That means one layer of silicon can only ever use about a third of the sunshine, even if I built it perfectly!

That means one layer of silicon can only ever grab about a third of the sunshine. Tiny coins, big coins, what a grumpy vending machine!
i4.checkRight: Coach, so light that is too weak just slips past the panel like a ghost through a door, and light that is too strong drops its extra energy as warm fuzz. That means one silicon layer only manages about a third of the sunshine, like a vending machine that refuses small coins and gives back the change from big ones. Right?
i4.why: Oh! So light that's too weak just zooms straight through my glass like a ghost, and light that's too strong spills its extra fizz as heat. Silicon wants just the right amount of energy to wake an electron, so most of the sunshine ends up as wasted sparkle!

i5.say: Ooh, so a panel likes to be cool, like my ink on a chilly day, because heat makes the atoms jiggle and that lowers the voltage. And it likes to face the Sun straight on, so it catches more of the little light packets, like a sunflower soaking up every drop!
i5.example: Oh! So a cold panel is happier, like my blot self on a cool damp page, because heat makes the atoms jiggle and lowers the voltage. And if a panel faces the Sun squarely, it catches more photons, like a puddle catching more rain when it sits flat on the ground!

i5.why: Oh! So a hot panel is like a fidgety crowd: the atoms jiggle, the voltage drops, and it works less well. A panel pointed straight at the Sun gets more photons, while a tilted one spreads the same light over more glass, like butter over too much toast!
i5.whyAsk: But WHY does a cool panel keep its voltage up, and why does squarely facing the Sun catch more photons? Is it the jiggling again?
i5.fixed: Oh! So panels don't get sunburnt or sulk, I had that wrong. Heat just makes the atoms jiggle and lowers the voltage, and a tilted beam spreads thinner over the glass. Cool and squarely aimed, got it!

script.text: When a photon carries enough energy, it hits a bond in the silicon and shakes one electron loose, which leaves an empty spot called a hole.
This is how light energy becomes moving charge, because a freed electron can travel through the crystal instead of staying stuck.
Where the two kinds of silicon touch, a permanent electric field forms, and it pushes freed electrons toward the n side and holes toward the p side.
No, the slope is not a playground slide for fun. It is an electric field at the p–n junction that sweeps charges apart so current can flow.
Without that push, freed electrons would drift randomly and recombine, so no steady current would run through the wire in a circuit.
A panel makes direct current that flows one way, but wall sockets give alternating current that reverses many times each second, and the inverter converts between them.
No, the inverter does not flip the panel upside down or run electricity backwards. It converts one-way direct current into back-and-forth alternating current.
Homes and the grid are built around alternating current, so panel power must be converted before ordinary appliances can safely use it.
Weak photons pass through without helping, and strong photons lose their extra energy as heat, so a single silicon layer converts only about a third of sunlight.
Silicon needs a certain amount of energy to free an electron, so photons that miss that amount are either useless or partly wasted.

i1.say: When a photon carries enough energy, it hits a bond in the silicon and shakes one electron loose, which leaves an empty spot called a hole.
i1.example: Think of a marble knocked out of its dent in a tray by a rolling ball; the marble can roll, and the dent stays behind.
i1.why: This is how light energy becomes moving charge, because a freed electron can travel through the crystal instead of staying stuck.
i1.fix: No, light is not bullets smashing the panel or making the glass bleed. It is photons freeing electrons from silicon bonds, leaving holes behind.

i2.say: Where the two kinds of silicon touch, a permanent electric field forms, and it pushes freed electrons toward the n side and holes toward the p side.
i2.example: Like a steady wind in a hallway that blows every leaf the same way, so a wire lets them circle back around.
i2.why: Without that push, freed electrons would drift randomly and recombine, so no steady current would run through the wire in a circuit.
i2.fix: No, the slope is not a playground slide for fun. It is an electric field at the p–n junction that sweeps charges apart so current can flow.

i3.say: A panel makes direct current that flows one way, but wall sockets give alternating current that reverses many times each second, and the inverter converts between them.
i3.example: Your phone battery gives steady one-way power, while the lamp plugged into the wall gets power that keeps switching direction.
i3.why: Homes and the grid are built around alternating current, so panel power must be converted before ordinary appliances can safely use it.
i3.fix: No, the inverter does not flip the panel upside down or run electricity backwards. It converts one-way direct current into back-and-forth alternating current.

i4.say: Weak photons pass through without helping, and strong photons lose their extra energy as heat, so a single silicon layer converts only about a third of sunlight.
i4.example: It is like a vending machine that ignores coins too small and keeps the change from coins too big.
i4.why: Silicon needs a certain amount of energy to free an electron, so photons that miss that amount are either useless or partly wasted.
i4.fix: No, panels are not lazy or sloppy, and they do not waste light on purpose. Physics limits one silicon layer to about a third of sunlight.

i5.say: Heat makes atoms jiggle and lowers a cell's voltage, so cooler panels work better, and a panel facing the Sun squarely catches more photons.
i5.example: A panel on a chilly bright day outperforms a hot roof one, and a flat-on panel beats one tilted away.
i5.why: Jiggling atoms disturb the electrons, and a slanted beam spreads over more glass, so each patch of panel receives fewer photons.
i5.fix: No, panels do not get sunburnt or sulk and hide from the Sun. Heat lowers voltage, and a tilted beam spreads thinner across the glass.
